Harry Freeman is a Head of AI who sets the strategy and can build it.
He decides where AI earns its place in a consultancy and its clients' work, then turns that into products, governance and new ways of working, and brings non-technical teams with him.
His rule is that AI supports expert judgement, and every output must be something a client or auditor can check.

Train a small transformer in your browser, on your GPU, with hand-written WebGPU kernels.
Watch the moment it learns to copy.
Then take it apart: knock out heads, patch activations between runs, and read its residual stream through a sparse autoencoder trained in WebGPU.
No server, no model download, no machine-learning library; the model you dissect is the one you just trained.
Open the page.
Within 150 ms a recorded run of this same code is on the trace, dim, marked REF.
Its blue copy loss falls off a cliff at step 1,500, labelled "recorded: L2·H4 learned to copy at step 1,500".
Your own run starts training over it in under a second.
Wait about 20–30 seconds.
Your run reaches the same cliff, and the trace writes it in orange: L2·H4 learned to copy at step 1,500 · copy loss 4.06 → 0.97 nats.
The head's lane under the trace turns orange, and its partner, a head that attends to the previous character, is outlined.
When the run ends, open Heads.
Shift-click the copying heads to knock them out.
On random characters shown twice, the trained model continues the copy 40 of 40 characters right; without those two heads, 0 of 40.
Open Features.
Pick a feature and pin it at three times its strongest activation.
Feature #918 fires on the "X" that starts the sonnets' Roman numerals; pinned, the model writes XXXXXXXX… and nothing else.
Olsson et al. 2022, In-context Learning and Induction Heads.
Every 20 training steps the GPU runs the standard test, between training steps and in the same command stream.
It takes 32 rows of 64 random characters, each shown twice.
For every head it measures the prefix-matching score: the attention each position of the second copy pays to the character just after the previous occurrence of its own character.
It also measures the previous-character score, and the loss on each copy.
A head counts as an induction head when its prefix-matching score reaches 0.3 and the second copy has become at least 1 nat easier than the first.
The first reading where that happens is the moment.
The trace marks it in words, draws the cliff in the copy loss (CH4) from the plateau, and lights the head's lane.
The scoring is three small WGSL kernels (probe_attn, probe_loss, plus a pattern copy) appended to a forward pass.
Their CPU reference is scoreProbe in src/model/probe.ts.
What it took to see the moment within a minute.
The finding first:
On text alone, no head learned to copy within the budget.
That held for 3,000 steps on the sonnets and 3,000 on the five tragedies.
A strong previous-character head formed on both, but no induction head.
Olsson et al. see the phase change after hundreds of millions of tokens; a minute here is about 7 million.
So one training window in four is random characters: a run of 12 to 48 characters, repeated to fill the window.
Nothing in it can be memorised, so the only way to predict a repeat is to copy it.
The period varies from window to window, so a head cannot pass by looking a fixed distance back.
The test uses runs of 64, longer than any repeat the model trained on.
The controls I ran, in this repository's tests/gpu/induction.html, with the probe on CPU snapshots:
text only (sonnets, tragedies), 3,000 steps · none
one window in four a repeated passage of the text · none in 1,700 steps (the model memorises the text, so copying never pays)
one in two: random characters with a fixed period of 64, no dropout, constant learning rate · at about step 2,850
one in eight: random characters, varying period · none in 2,000 steps
one in four: random characters, varying period (shipped) · step 1,100–1,600 across the seeds and dropout settings tried; 1,500 for the shipped seed
Training is deterministic for a seed on a given GPU.
The live run and the recorded one both found L2·H4 at step 1,500, with its partner L1·H2 attending to the previous character (score 0.99).
When the run ends, the GPU repeats the forward pass with a head_edit kernel spliced in before each layer's output projection.
The kernel scales each head's output (0 knocks it out) and can add the same head's output saved from another run.
Knockout (zero-ablation): for each of the 16 heads, the change in loss on held-out text and on the test's second copy.
Activation patching (Meng et al. 2022, and as used by Olsson et al.):
Clean run: the test.
Corrupted run: the first copy replaced with other random characters, so the second copy has nothing to copy from.
Patched runs: the corrupted run, once per head, with that head's output taken from the clean run, measuring how much of the copying returns.
Results on the shipped run (step 2,250):
L1·H2 · previous character (1.00) · +4.65 nats · +0.84 · −5%

facts.text: Read together: the induction heads carry the copy, and they depend on the previous-character head.
Patching the previous-character head alone restores nothing, because the head that copies still reads the corrupted first copy.
The page also lets you knock heads out while the model writes.
Generation runs on the CPU in workers, through a key/value-cache decoder with the same hooks.
One demonstration does it on random characters shown twice, continued greedily: 40 of 40 right as trained, 0 of 40 with L2·H3 and L2·H4 knocked out.
Bricken et al. 2023, Towards Monosemanticity; Cunningham et al. 2023, Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models.
After the run, the trained model reads the whole training text in consecutive windows.
The residual stream entering its last block is kept at every position: 86,016 vectors of 128.
Shape: an autoencoder with 1,024 features (8×) learns to rebuild those vectors: f = ReLU(x·W_enc + b_enc), x̂ = f·W_dec + b_dec.
Loss: squared error plus λ = 2 times the sum of activations.
Inputs are scaled so the average vector has squared length 128.
Training: Adam, 3,000 steps of 4,096 vectors, with the decoder rows renormalised to unit length after every step.
It takes about 9 seconds.
Everything runs on the GPU:
the existing tiled matmul and AdamW kernels;
new kernels for the random row gather, the ReLU, the loss gradients, decoder normalisation and error sums;
a top-k kernel that scans every position for each feature's 12 strongest contexts and its firing count.
Measured on the shipped run: 15.0% of the residual stream's variance unexplained; 14.7 features active per character on average; 0.0% dead features (none that never fires).
These are fidelity numbers, not a quality score.
I did not measure the loss with the reconstruction spliced back into the model ("loss recovered").
Labels are by rule, never by a model.
Each candidate rule is a test on one context:
the character itself, or the one before or after it;
the word it is in, or the word just before it;
the start or end of a word or line, capitals, vowels, punctuation.
A feature's label is the most specific rule, or pair of rules, that holds for at least 9 of its 12 strongest contexts, with specificity discounted by coverage.
It is shown with its count: "holds for 12 of the 12 strongest contexts".
675 of the 1,024 features get a label; the rest are shown as examples only.
Typical labels: "“t” ending a word", "“u” after “r”", "the space after “and”", "“X” after a line break".
Pinning a feature while the model writes: at the residual stream entering the last block, the decoder adds (value − f_j(x)) · d_j.
That sets feature j to the chosen value and leaves everything the autoencoder does not explain untouched (clampFeature in src/cpu/sae.ts).

Discrete semantic entropy, adapted from Farquhar, Kossen, Kuhn and Gal, Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy, Nature (2024).
Five independent answers are sampled from Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct.
DeBERTa xsmall NLI tests each pair in both directions.
Complete-link grouping requires every within-group pair to entail both ways at a fixed 0.60 threshold.
Entropy is −Σ p log₂ p, using each group's empirical share of five answers.
Our conservative grouping differs from the paper's representative-based implementation.
Token confidence is the original untempered model softmax probability, captured before repetition penalty, temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling.
The displayed answer summary is a geometric mean.
Entropy measures disagreement, not truth: a model can confidently repeat a falsehood.
The additional forced binary claim verdict uses (1 + mean(entailment − contradiction)) / 2 ≥ 0.50, separately from entropy.
That authored support index is not a calibrated truth probability.
The checked source remains authoritative.
Transformers.js was chosen because it exposes causal-model logits and NLI in a browser worker.
Generation uses WebGPU; NLI uses one WebAssembly thread.
WebKit isolates NLI in a second CPU-only ONNX Runtime worker to make persisted cached reload reliable; Chromium uses one combined worker.
The official browser-only SDK is vendored without native image dependencies; ONNX Runtime is pinned separately.

Great Britain's electricity grid, played live as an orchestral score.

Each source of power has its own staff and its own voice: wind is a string pad, solar rings bells, gas holds a low drone, nuclear keeps a steady pulse, hydro runs like water, biomass sings, imports arrive as distant chords, and coal (should it ever return) is grit.
Each plays louder the bigger its share of generation, and carbon intensity chooses the key: a clean grid plays in bright modes, a dirty one turns minor.
The score is engraved as you listen, a note inked the moment it sounds.
Pick any day since 12 May 2018 and the page presses it as a record: a minute of audio rendered in your browser, with the day's own score as its sleeve.

The page fetches that day from NESO (two requests; yesterday is already on the page and costs none), composes it one bar an hour (23, 24 or 25 bars, whatever the clocks did), engraves the sleeve, then renders the same bars offline with the same engine the page plays live, faster than real time.
You get:
a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz stereo WAV of about a minute, with its title, artist, date and data credit inside it (RIFF INFO and an ID3 tag) and the sleeve embedded as cover art;
the sleeve as a 2400 px PNG: the day's score as the first page of a printed edition, in three systems of eight bars (night, day, evening), each bar labelled with its hour;
liner notes on the page: how many half-hours NESO had, the cleanest hour, the journey of keys.
The same date and place always press the same record.

Rendering takes about 3 seconds in WebKit, 5 to 12 seconds in Chromium and about a minute in Firefox, whose offline audio runs at roughly real time (it shows a running count instead of a percentage, since Firefox doesn't report progress).
An ossia is the engraver's alternative passage, printed in small staves above the music.
Press Ossia: fully renewable (or O) and the moment you are hearing is re-scored for a hypothetical grid that runs on wind, sun and water alone:
gas, coal, nuclear, biomass, imports and other are set to zero, and their share is handed to wind, solar and hydro in proportion to each one's real share that half-hour (src/music/ossia.ts);
if a half-hour had no wind, sun or water at all, there is nothing to scale up, so the ossia gives the whole grid to wind, the renewable that can run at any hour;
NESO's factors for wind, solar and hydro are 0 g CO₂/kWh, so the ossia is 0 g and the key ladder puts it in D Lydian, luminoso.
Both versions of every bar are always composed, by two conductors in step, so switching is instant and mid-bar: the sound changes without a restart and you hear the same moment real and renewable.

The ossia is printed over the live bar (over every bar of a replayed day), labelled ossia: fully renewable, hypothetical, and the rule and its numbers (real mix against ossia mix, real grams against 0 g, real key against Lydian) appear under the controls.
It never appears in the Live label or the live bar's time.

Pressed with the ossia on, a record is the ossia's: its sleeve engraves only wind, solar and hydro, says ossia and hypothetical and marks the other parts tacet, and its file names and tags say so too.
Louder sounds better to most ears, and the ossia, with its big wind and solar parts and a brighter key, measures 1.8 to 2.7 LU louder than the real grid across the sample day.

So the two are loudness-matched before you compare them, with the broadcast standard's integrated loudness, ITU-R BS.1770-4 (src/audio/loudness.ts): K-weighting (a high shelf for the head and a 38 Hz high pass), mean square over 400 ms blocks overlapping by 75%, an absolute gate at −70 LUFS and a relative gate 10 LU below, then the gated mean.
It is tested against the standard's own 48 kHz filter coefficients and the EBU Tech 3341 reference signals (cases 1 to 4, both gates).
Live, per moment (src/audio/match.ts, src/ossia-loudness.ts).

When the ossia is on, the page renders the moment both ways offline, in your browser, sixteen bars each at 48 kHz, measures each, and trims the ossia to the real grid's loudness; the real grid keeps its own level.
A replay is matched hour by hour, measuring the next hour ahead.

While listening to the real grid it measures in the background, so switching is usually matched at once; until a moment is measured the last trim carries over, or, before any, the typical −2.2 dB, labelled provisional.
The arithmetic runs in a worker.
A measurement takes about 1.5 to 7 seconds depending on the browser and the machine, and the panel shows both loudnesses, the trims and the time it took.
How fair.

At every other half-hour of the sample day the page's own measurement set the trim, and an independent render of the same moment (other notes) checked it: the trimmed ossia and the real grid differ by 0.06 LU at the median and 0.25 LU at most (node scripts/measure-audio.mjs --loudness).

An interactive calculation pad where every number carries a unit, a source and, if it is uncertain, a cited or assumed spread.

The answer is then a distribution, not one number: drag a quantity and 4,096 Monte Carlo runs redraw in the same frame; let go and 100,000 runs and a variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity analysis show which uncertainty actually matters.

Monte Carlo propagation (JCGM 101:2008, the GUM’s Supplement 1).
Each run draws every uncertain input from its declared distribution and recomputes the whole program; the spread of answers is the result’s distribution.
The page reports P5, P50 and P95 (Hyndman and Fan’s type-7 quantiles, the R and NumPy default), the mean, and the answer from central inputs, all in the result’s own unit.
The trick that makes 100,000 runs cheap is that units are static.

The checker has already proven every dimension, so src/analysis/columns.ts evaluates the checked syntax tree once per operation over a whole column of runs (Float64Arrays), resolving each unit conversion once instead of 100,000 times.

It mirrors the interpreter’s arithmetic in the same order, and a test proves it reproduces the scalar interpreter bit for bit on every example, including decimal rounding (a fast path defers to the interpreter’s exact routine near ties).
A run that divides by zero or takes a negative square root is counted as undefined and excluded, never folded into the answer.
One literal is one random variable, even when a function uses it twice.

Variance-based sensitivity (Sobol′ 2001; Saltelli et al. 2010; Jansen 1999).
The tornado nudges one input at a time by ±5, 10 or 20%.
The variance share asks a different question: how much of the result’s spread comes from each input’s declared uncertainty.

With two independent sample matrices A and B and, for each input i, A with column i taken from B, the first-order index Sᵢ = mean(f(B)·(f(A_Bⁱ) − f(A)))/V (Saltelli 2010) is the share of variance that knowing input i exactly would remove; the total index Sₜᵢ = mean((f(A) − f(A_Bⁱ))²)/2V (Jansen 1999) adds every interaction it takes part in.
The hatched gap between them is interaction.
Outputs are centred first, as Sobol′ recommends; intervals are 95% percentile bootstraps over 100 resamples.
The design costs (k + 2) × 16,384 runs for k uncertain inputs.
Fixed inputs say “fixed”: they have no variance to share.
A rule-written sentence above the table states the finding from the numbers on screen.

The limits of the method are stated on the page: inputs are sampled independently (correlations are not modelled), and a distribution is only as good as the spreads declared, which are labelled cited or assumed wherever they appear.

The tests check the engine against closed forms rather than against itself: a sum of normals in mixed units (km + mi) reproduces its analytic P5/P50/P95 within the quantile standard error; a product of lognormals reproduces its analytic quantiles and mean within 1%; Sobol indices recover an additive model (S = T = ⅕, ⅘, 0) and the product X₁·X₂ of normals, whose interaction is exact (S₁ = 0.889, S₂ = 0.056, T₁ = 0.944, T₂ = 0.111), within 0.03; every distribution reproduces its exact mean and variance; the two-piece normal puts 95% of 200,000 draws between its limits (binomial tolerance); and the xoshiro128** outputs for state (1, 2, 3, 4) match hand-derived reference values.

ask-the-record is a question box for a personal site, a documentation page or a project page that never writes an answer.
Every reply is a quote from your own content, word for word, with the matching words marked, the strength of the match shown, and a link to where it came from.
When nothing in the content supports an answer, it says "No source for that." and shows the numbers behind that decision.
Retrieval runs in the visitor's browser, so their question never leaves the page.
A generated answer has to be checked against its source; a quote is the source, so a reader can check it in one click.
You need Node.js 22 or later.
From a clone of this repository:

npm ci
npm run build
npm run demo
Then open http://127.0.0.1:4310/ to ask this README questions.
The page shows this file line by line, as its own source.
Asking a question marks the passage that answers it in place, writes the question in the margin beside it, and places the question on a map of the README's facts.
The demo's record is built from this file, so it can only answer what is written here.
The demo also takes your own markdown: choose "Use your own markdown", paste a page, and the record is built, embedded and searched in your browser, with nothing uploaded.
The docs page, at http://127.0.0.1:4310/docs/, lists every attribute, event and part next to a live specimen.
To put a question box on your own page, build a record from your markdown.
The repository has a small example about page to try it on:

node dist/cli.js build examples/about.md -o examples/record.json --embed
node dist/cli.js ask examples/record.json "Which street is the studio on?"
node dist/cli.js ask examples/record.json --hybrid "Can I park there?"
With npm run demo still running, http://127.0.0.1:4310/examples/ shows that record in a page with nothing else on it.
The whole integration is two lines of HTML:

<script type="module" src="ask-the-record.min.js"></script>
<ask-the-record src="record.json"></ask-the-record>
When the page also uses the map or the ranks view, the script loads ask-the-record-explain.min.js from beside itself, so the embed stays one script tag.
For your own page, build from your own markdown and copy dist/ask-the-record.min.js and the record next to the page.
The package is not published to npm yet, so these commands run the built CLI from the clone.
The --embed flag downloads the embedding model once (about 24 MB) and runs it on your machine.
Without --embed, the record still works: keyword search is instant, and the browser embeds the facts itself once the model has loaded.
A record is your markdown, split into facts.
Each fact is one sentence, list item, table row or short code block, with the section it sits in and the line it starts on.
The fact keeps the exact text a reader sees, with the markdown syntax removed and nothing reworded.
The build step parses the markdown, gives every fact a stable id, and writes record.json.
A fact's id is its section's anchor plus a hash of its text, so it survives edits to the sentences around it.
Identical sentences in one section are told apart by number, in order.
With --embed, every fact is embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and stored as 384 signed bytes, and a t-SNE layout of the facts is computed for the optional map.
When the page loads, the element fetches record.json and validates it before using any of it.
Validation checks the schema and the record's own consistency: references in range, ids unique, vectors of the right size, and embeddings built for exactly these facts.
An invalid record is reported as an error, never answered from.
Keyword search works as soon as the record has loaded.
Keyword search uses BM25 over English words, with stop words removed and Porter stemming, so "refusal" matches "refuses".
Section titles and table headings count at half weight, so a fact is found by the heading it sits under.
Code blocks also count at half weight, with each word counted once, because code repeats its keywords.
Meaning search starts when the visitor first focuses the question box.

A Web Worker loads transformers.js and the model, tries WebGPU first and WebAssembly second, and trusts a backend only after it reproduces two of the record's stored vectors to a cosine of at least 0.95.
In testing in Chromium, WebAssembly and WebGPU reproduced them to cosines between 0.985 and 0.993.
After that, only the question is embedded; comparing it with every fact is a single pass of dot products.
A model that is already running is checked the same way before it serves a different record.
The two rankings are combined by reciprocal rank fusion with k = 10.
A fact's fused score is the sum of 1 / (k + rank) over the keyword ranking and the meaning ranking.
The refusal policy then decides whether anything supports an answer.
The policy answers on meaning when the closest fact has a cosine of at least 0.48.
The policy answers on keywords when one fact holds at least 60% of the question's words, weighted by how rare each word is, and that same fact has a cosine of at least 0.30.
The meaning bar rises by 0.08 when the question uses a word the record never does.
In every other case it refuses and says which number fell short.
When typing pauses, the box previews the answer it would give; pressing Enter asks, and only an asked question is announced or refused.
An answer is up to three facts, quoted verbatim, best first.
When the answer rests on meaning, each quoted fact needs a cosine within 0.10 of the closest fact, or the question's keywords and a cosine of at least 0.30.
When it rests on keywords, each quoted fact needs both.
The words that matched the question are marked, and words that matched through a configured synonym are marked differently.
Each quote shows its section, a similarity score or the count of matched words, and a link to its source.
After a meaning answer, the box shows which words the match leaned on.
Each quoted fact is embedded again with one word removed at a time, and the words whose removal costs the most similarity are underlined, more heavily the more they cost.
The underline measures the model's sensitivity to a word, which is evidence for a reader to weigh, not an explanation of the model.
Without a --source URL, quotes link to the section's anchor on the page that hosts the box.
With --source, quotes link to that page, and a text fragment scrolls to and highlights the quoted sentence itself.
Quoting is the default, and it stays instant.
On top of it, <ask-the-record-verify for="ask"> writes an answer in its own words and then proves each sentence against the record, in the browser, sentence by sentence, as the answer is written.
A sentence the record does not back is struck out where it stands, with its score, and an answer with nothing left standing becomes a refusal.
The writer is Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct, a small open instruct model.
The writer reads the four source lines the quotes came from and writes two or three sentences.
The checker is DeBERTa-v3 xsmall, a natural language inference (NLI) model trained on SNLI and MultiNLI, which scores whether one text entails, contradicts or is neutral to another.
The checker runs in a second worker, so every sentence is checked as soon as it is finished, while the next is still being written.
Each sentence is compared with the six retrieved record sentences that share most of its words, and with the whole paragraph of the best of them, and the best entailment counts.
That comparison against each premise sentence is the zero-shot method of SummaC (Laban et al. 2022).
Support is looked for among the retrieved passages, as in the research step of RARR (Gao et al. 2023), rather than taken from the model's own citations, because a model this small cites unreliably.
Using NLI to judge whether a sentence is attributable to its source follows AIS (Rashkin et al. 2023) and TRUE (Honovich et al. 2022).
Scoring an answer sentence by sentence, against hand labels, follows FActScore (Min et al. 2023); answering with attributions is the setting of Attributed QA (Bohnet et al. 2022).
A sentence stands only when its best entailment is at least 0.90 and beats contradiction against the same record sentence.
A sentence a record sentence contradicts is marked as contradicted, and any other unsupported sentence as unsupported.
A sentence too short to stand alone, such as "Yes", is shown but never counted as an answer.
Each kept sentence links to the line that supports it, and with highlight set, that record sentence is underlined in the page.
The two models are 889 MB together: 793 MB for the writer and 96 MB for the checker.
Nothing is downloaded until the visitor asks, and the size is shown before the download starts.
Progress is shown as it goes, and the download can be cancelled at any moment.
A failed download is reported in plain words, and the quotes keep answering.
The weights stay in the browser's Cache API, so a second visit downloads nothing; with cache="none" they are kept for one visit only.
The writer runs on WebGPU when its backend passes a check, and on WebAssembly otherwise, which is much slower.
On a phone, the box offers the download with a warning, and the recorded runs still play.

Until the models are loaded, recorded runs of this same code are replayed at the speed they ran, and labelled as recorded. npm run verify:record records them in headless Chromium, and the demo's five suggested questions are chosen to show each outcome.
npm run verify:record -- --eval writes an answer for every question in the evaluation set and records every token and score.
Each sentence the writer drafted was then labelled once, by hand, as supported by this README or not.
A sentence counts as supported only if every part of it is in the README, so one wrong number or one added claim makes it unsupported.
The builder of this repository (Claude, an AI assistant) did the labelling, before looking at the checker's verdicts.
The labels are in eval/verify-labels.json, each with its exact sentence, for anyone to audit.
The entailment bar was chosen on the development half alone, from 0.5 to 0.95, as the one whose kept sentences were most often truly supported.
The held-out half was scored once the bar was fixed. npm run verify:score reproduces the table; two other checkers were scored on the very same sentences with npm run verify:rescore.
The percentages are followed by their counts and 95% Wilson intervals.

facts.text: The writer is the weak part: unchecked, only 8 of the 60 sentences it drafted are supported by the README.
With the checker, 3 of the 9 sentences kept on the development half were supported, and 3 of the 3 kept on the held-out half; 20 of the 22 unanswerable questions were refused.
The sentences it wrongly kept change a number slightly (795 MB for 793 MB), lift a phrase of the README out of context, or misread a passage.
Neither of the other two checkers did better on the held-out half, and the larger one, DeBERTa-v3 base, kept more unsupported sentences there.
The counts are small, so the intervals are wide, and most answerable questions end in a refusal: the checker trades answers for being right.
The element is <ask-the-record>, a framework-free custom element that renders into Shadow DOM.
src · URL of the record.json to load. Required.
model · Embedding model id, or none for keyword search only. Defaults to the model the record was embedded with.
model-host · Base URL for model files, for self-hosting. Defaults to the Hugging Face Hub.
model-dtype · Model weights to load when the record has no embeddings. Defaults to q8.
runtime · URL of the transformers.js ES module. Defaults to a pinned version on jsDelivr.
live · Preview answers while the visitor types. Previews are never announced or refused.
label · Visible label for the question box. Defaults to "Ask a question".
placeholder · Placeholder text for the question box.
highlight · A CSS selector. Each answer is also marked inside the element it names, using the CSS Custom Highlight API.
highlight-scroll · With highlight, scroll the first quote into view.
With model="none", the element makes no requests beyond record.json.
A change to model, model-host, model-dtype or runtime takes effect at once, without fetching the record again.
Anything placed in the element's suggestions slot, such as example questions, is shown between the status line and the answer.
The element's ask(question) method puts a question in the box, asks it, and resolves with the result.
Given a vector, as in ask(question, { vector }), the element uses that embedding instead of running the model; the vector must come from the record's own model.
A supplied vector is refused when the record has no stored vectors, when its size is wrong, or when the facts are being searched with vectors that another model computed in the browser.
The demo embeds its suggested questions when the page is built, so its first answer needs no download.
The element's load(record) method takes a record object instead of fetching src, validates it exactly as a fetched one, and throws on an invalid record.
A record built in the page has no vectors, so the model the element is already running embeds its facts in the browser.
dist/ask-the-record-build.min.js is the markdown parser and the quotability linter for the browser, about 23 KB gzipped, for pages that let visitors try their own content.
The demo loads it only when someone does.
The element's record, result, modelState and diagnostics properties expose what it loaded, what it answered and how the model was checked.
The element's thresholds property overrides the refusal policy, which you should do when you use a different embedding model.
The element dispatches these events, all of which bubble out of the Shadow DOM:
ask-the-record:ready · The record has loaded and validated. detail.record is the record.
ask-the-record:status · The model's state changed. detail.text is the status line shown.
ask-the-record:answer · A question was answered or refused. detail.result is the full result. An empty question is ignored.
ask-the-record:preview · With live, a preview was shown while typing. detail.result is the result.
ask-the-record:vectors · The facts of a record without vectors were embedded in the browser. detail.vectors holds them.
ask-the-record:located · With highlight, an answer was looked for in the page. detail.located lists each quote found, with its Range; detail.highlighted is false where the Highlight API is missing.
ask-the-record:leans · Attribution finished. detail.leans maps each quote to the words its meaning match leaned on.
ask-the-record:clear · The answer on show was cleared, by Escape or an emptied box.
ask-the-record:source · A quote's source link was clicked. Call preventDefault() to handle it yourself.
ask-the-record:error · The record could not be loaded, or asking failed unexpectedly. detail.error is the error.
The element inherits the page's font and text colour.
Every colour is derived from the page's own text colour unless you set it.

You can restyle it with these CSS custom properties: --atr-accent, --atr-color, --atr-muted, --atr-rule, --atr-mark, --atr-mark-related, --atr-font, --atr-quote-font, --atr-mono-font, --atr-input-size, --atr-quote-size, --atr-gap and --atr-focus.

For anything else, every piece is exposed with ::part(): form, label, field, input, submit, status, load, answer, summary, quotes, quote, quote-context, quote-text, passage, code, mark, lean, legend, pending, quote-meta, source, strength, strength-label, meter, meter-fill, meter-mark, refusal, refusal-title, refusal-reason, closest and error.
The question box has a visible label, and Enter asks the question.
Escape clears the box and the answer.
Each answer or refusal is announced through a polite live region: the number of quotes and the first quote, or the refusal and its reason.
Every link in an answer is reachable with the Tab key.
Animation is skipped when the visitor prefers reduced motion, and marks stay visible in Windows high-contrast mode.
<ask-the-record-verify for="ask"> follows the <ask-the-record id="ask"> it names, like the map.

The verify element's attributes are recordings (a JSON file of recorded runs to replay), model-host and runtime (to host the models and transformers.js yourself), cache="none", and highlight (a selector: each supporting record sentence is underlined there).
The element's start() loads the models and cancel() stops a download or a run at once.

The element dispatches ask-the-record-verify:state, ask-the-record-verify:sentence (each verdict, with its line), ask-the-record-verify:cite (a line number was followed) and ask-the-record-verify:done.
The file is dist/ask-the-record-verify.min.js, about 20 KB gzipped, and the single script loads it when the page uses the element.

With highlight="#article", every answer is also marked inside the element that selector names, without adding any markup: the quoted passages, the question's words in them, and, once attribution has run, the words the meaning match leaned on.
A refusal marks its closest passage instead.
Each mark is a named highlight for the page to style: ::highlight(ask-the-record), ::highlight(ask-the-record-words), ::highlight(ask-the-record-leans) and ::highlight(ask-the-record-closest).

A page that draws its markdown as source lines can mark each line with data-record-line, and then each fact is found on exactly the line it starts on; otherwise a fact is looked for in its section, by heading id.
To make the page the only place an answer shows, hide the element's own answer with ask-the-record::part(answer) { display: none; }.
The demo works that way.
<ask-the-record-map for="ask"> draws the record as points, one per fact, next to the <ask-the-record id="ask"> it names.
With a record built using --embed, facts are placed by meaning, using a t-SNE layout computed at build time; otherwise they are grouped by section.
When a question is answered, the quoted facts are marked, so you can see where in the record the answer came from.

A t-SNE layout cannot place a new point exactly, so the question is drawn at the centre of its five nearest facts by meaning, weighted by similarity squared, with a line to each fact it quoted, and the caption says so.

A refused question is drawn outside the cloud, beyond its nearest facts, and further out the further its closest fact fell short of the bar, with dotted lines to its three nearest facts and their scores.

For a record of up to 1,000 facts without a layout, such as one built in the page, the map runs t-SNE in the browser once the facts are embedded, a slice per animation frame, and then moves the points to their places by meaning.

<ask-the-record-ranks for="ask"> shows how an answer was decided: the facts ranked by shared words (BM25) and by meaning (cosine) side by side, a line joining each fact that appears in both, and the fused order the quotes were taken from.
The rankings appear in that order, words first.
Both views are in dist/ask-the-record-explain.min.js, which dist/ask-the-record.min.js loads by itself when the page uses either one.
The question is never sent anywhere.
The question is embedded in a Web Worker on the visitor's device and compared with the record in the page.
By default, the model files are downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub and the runtime from jsDelivr, so those services see the visitor's IP address, but never the question.
To avoid third-party requests, host the runtime and the model files yourself and set runtime and model-host, or use model="none".
The browser caches the model after the first visit.
On a connection that asks to save data, the model is not downloaded until the visitor chooses to load it.
On a page with a Content Security Policy, the element needs worker-src blob: for its model worker, on top of wherever its script and record.json are served from ('self' on your own site).
With the default runtime and model, it also needs script-src https://cdn.jsdelivr.net 'wasm-unsafe-eval' and connect-src https://cdn.jsdelivr.net https://huggingface.co https://*.hf.co.

The demo page's whole policy is default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; worker-src blob:; connect-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net https://huggingface.co https://*.hf.co; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'.
The element's styles are constructed stylesheets, so style-src needs no 'unsafe-inline', and script-src needs no blob:.
When the worker is blocked, the element says so and keeps answering by keywords.
The record format is versioned, and this is version 1; the element rejects any other version.
The JSON Schema for record.json is in schema/record.schema.json, and every record is checked against it when it is built and when it is loaded.
A record holds a title, a language, an optional source URL, optional synonym groups, the sections, and the facts.
Each fact has an id, its text, its kind (text, item, row or code), its section, and the line in the markdown it came from.
A record built with --embed also holds the model name, the int8 vectors with one scale per fact, and a hash of the exact text that was embedded.
A record built with --embed that has between 5 and 3,000 facts also holds the map layout.
Facts are quoted exactly as written, so write sentences that stand on their own.
A sentence that starts with "It" or "This" reads poorly as a quote, because its subject is in the sentence before.

check <record.json> · Validates a record and summarises it.
lint <record.md> · Reports facts that will read badly as quotes: ones that start with a pronoun, are very short or very long, or repeat.
ask <record.json> <question> · Asks a record from the terminal; --hybrid embeds the question too, and --json prints the full result.
explain <record.json> <question> · Shows the working: the top facts by fused rank, every score, which were quoted, and why the policy answered or refused.
eval <record.json> <questions.json> · Scores a record on your own labelled questions; --min-precision turns it into a check for continuous integration.
The explain command shows the working behind an answer.

A questions file is a JSON list of objects, each with a question and, for questions the record should answer, a support list of passages any one of which makes a quote correct.

The build command takes these options: --title, --source, --language en or --language none, --synonyms with a JSON file of word groups, --embed, and with --embed also --model, --dtype, --pooling, --query-prefix, --passage-prefix and --no-map.

npm run eval asks this README a labelled set of questions and reports how often it answers when it should and refuses when it should.
Some questions are answerable from the README, and some are not, including questions about nearby topics the README never covers and requests to write something.
An answer counts as correct only if one of its quotes contains a passage the question was labelled with.
Answer precision is the share of answers that were correct.
Answer recall is the share of answerable questions answered correctly.
Refusal precision is the share of refusals that were right to refuse.
Refusal recall is the share of unanswerable questions that were refused.
The thresholds were set by hand while looking only at the development half of the questions.
The held-out half was written at the same time and scored once the thresholds were fixed, so it is the fairer measure.

facts.text: On answers, the two halves score within a few points of each other; on refusals, the held-out half is lower in both modes.
Most wrong answers quote a passage on the right topic that does not answer the question.
Most answerable questions that were refused use words the README does not, which meaning search only partly makes up for.
Both modes refuse nearly every unanswerable question, and keyword search answers fewer of the answerable ones than hybrid search does.
Hybrid results use question embeddings computed in Node and stored in eval/question-vectors.json, so the evaluation runs offline and gives the same numbers every time.
A browser can compute slightly different vectors, so its answers can differ at the margins.
Quoting instead of generating means every answer can be checked, because every answer is the source.
A summary would read better, but a reader would have to trust it.
Written answers are opt-in and checked because a fluent answer is easy to trust and hard to verify.
Checking every sentence against the record, and striking what fails, keeps the property the quotes have: every claim left on screen points to the line that supports it.
Refusing is the default, and a refusal shows the number that fell short and the bar it missed.
A refusal with its reasons is as useful as an answer, because it tells the reader the content does not say.
Keyword search comes first because it is instant, needs no download, and still works when the model cannot load.
Meaning search is added on top of it, never instead of it.
A backend is used only after it reproduces the record's own vectors, because WebGPU can run a model and still return wrong numbers on some devices.
A backend that fails the check is skipped, and when WebGPU fails it, the browser remembers not to try WebGPU again for that model.
Facts are sentence-sized because a quote should be short enough to read at a glance and specific enough to answer one question.
The demo marks answers in the README itself, not in a separate answer box, because a quote is easiest to judge in its context, with the sentences around it right there to read.
The linter exists because the quality of the answers depends on the writing.
A sentence that leans on the one before it is a poor quote, so lint finds those sentences before a visitor does.
This README passes its own linter, and a test keeps it that way.
Attribution works by occlusion because any embedding model supports it, and its claim is narrow enough to be true: these are the words the similarity depended on.
Attribution costs one extra embedding per word of each quoted fact, so it runs only after an asked question is answered, never while typing.
Vectors are stored as int8 with one scale per fact, which is a quarter of the size of float32.
For 384-dimension unit vectors, the stored vectors keep cosine scores within 0.01 of the originals.
Every input from outside the code is parsed before it is trusted: the record, the markdown parser's tokens, the model's output, and the worker's messages.
The browser bundle has one runtime dependency, valibot, used to validate the record.

The core plus the element is about 27 KB gzipped, without transformers.js, which the worker loads only when it is needed. npm run size, which runs in continuous integration, fails if it grows past 30 KB.
Retrieval is not understanding.
A quote can share words or meaning with a question without answering it, and the box cannot tell the difference.
The reader decides whether a quote answers the question.
The answers are only as good as the record.
If the record is out of date or wrong, the quotes are too.
Keyword search knows English.
With --language none, words are matched without stop words or stemming.
Chinese, Japanese and other languages written without spaces are not split into words, so keyword search works poorly for them.
The thresholds suit all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and records like this README.
A different model, or very different content, needs its own thresholds.
BM25 ignores word order and negation, so "does not" and "does" look the same to keyword search.
Everything is held in memory and every fact is scored for every question, which suits a page or a small set of documents, up to a few thousand facts, not a search engine.
The checker is a small NLI model, and it errs both ways: it has kept sentences the README does not support, and struck sentences it does.
A kept sentence comes with its score and the line it rests on, as evidence for a reader to weigh, not as a guarantee.
Attribution shows sensitivity, not reasoning.
An underlined word is one whose removal lowered the similarity, which is not the same as the reason a person would give.
The first visit downloads about 29 MB before meaning search is ready: 23 MB of model weights and 6 MB of WebAssembly runtime.
Later visits load them from the browser's cache, which took under a second in testing.
ask-the-record is not a chatbot: it has no memory of earlier questions, it cannot follow up, and it never writes new text.

Your coding agent proposes changes to its own memory each night; you measure them, check them against everything else it remembers, and review them like a pull request.
Coding agents such as Claude Code keep long-term memory as plain files that are loaded into every session.
Those files are either written by hand, which goes stale, or written by the agent unsupervised, which accumulates guesses nobody checked. dreaming sits between the two.

After you log off, a headless agent with read-only tools re-reads the day's sessions and proposes what memory should learn, correct or forget, citing quotes that dreaming checks against the transcripts.

Then dreaming does two things no memory system does for you: it measures a proposal, by running a task suite with and without it in isolated agent sessions and reporting the change in pass rate, turns and tokens with honest intervals; and it checks every proposal for contradictions with the rest of your memory, with a small language-inference model running on your machine.
In the morning you approve, edit or reject, with all of that beside each proposal.
Only approved changes are written, with a backup and an audit trail.
The agent proposes; the evidence is checked; a person approves.
A memory is an instruction your agent will follow in every session from now on. dreaming treats a proposed one the way you would treat a code change: it runs the tests.

The experiment.

A task suite is a template repository, a few everyday tasks, and for each task a check the agent never sees. dreaming runs every task the same number of times in two arms: without the proposal (the memory directory as it is now) and with it (the same directory with the proposal applied by the same planner the real apply uses, so the agent sees exactly what approving would write).
The arms differ in nothing else: same prompts, same model, same fresh copy of the repository, in a seeded random order so time-of-day drift falls on both.
Each run is a real claude -p session; afterwards the task's check decides pass or fail and says why ("ran npm install (1×), which breaks the workspace links").
An eval makes at most 30 runs.
The statistics are chosen for small samples, because 30 runs is a small sample:
each arm's pass rate gets the Clopper–Pearson exact interval (Clopper and Pearson, 1934), which never undercovers;

the change in pass rate gets Newcombe's hybrid score interval for a difference of proportions (Newcombe, 1998, method 10), which behaves at 0/5 and 5/5 where the textbook interval collapses (it is tested against the paper's worked examples);

each task is its own comparison, so a task counts as moved only when Fisher's exact test (Fisher, 1922) is below 0.05/k and its interval, made simultaneous at 1 − 0.05/k with a Bonferroni correction (Dunn, 1961), clears zero.
With three tasks that is 98.3% each, so a chance "effect" on one of them does not turn up one eval in seven.

Both rules were added after the real runs showed why: a tabs memory "helped" a package-manager task by 0/5 → 3/5, and in another batch "hurt" it by 5/5 → 1/5, where the approximate interval clears zero and the exact test (p = 0.048) does not;
turns, tokens and time get a stratified percentile bootstrap of the difference in means (Efron, 1979), resampled within each task, with a seeded generator so a replay prints the same numbers.
The approach follows Miller (2024), "Adding Error Bars to Evals": report the interval, not the point; compare arms on the same questions; plan for the sample you can afford.

A memory is flagged worse when any task moved down by that rule, and helps when one moved up; otherwise the verdict is "no measurable effect", with the intervals, because that is what five runs per arm per task can say.
The pooled interval across tasks is shown for context but does not decide: it mixes tasks with different base rates.

Isolation, proved rather than assumed.
Eval runs must not touch your setup, and your hooks must not run (yours might play sounds).

Every run gets --safe-mode (installed plugins, hooks, CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers off), --setting-sources project (no user or local settings; the temporary repository has none), --settings with disableAllHooks plus a canary hook on every hook event that would touch a file if any hook ran at all, --strict-mcp-config, --no-session-persistence (no transcript, so no dream ever reads an eval), an environment built from an allowlist (nothing of your session's variables), a working directory outside your home, and the memory in a mode-0600 file (--append-system-prompt-file), never in argv, where any process listing would show it.
Then the proof, recorded in every eval:
A positive control.
Before any run, Claude Code starts with the canary hook enabled, in an empty, separate config directory (no login, no plugins, no model call).

The canary must fire and Claude Code must report the hook events in its stream (--include-hook-events); otherwise the eval refuses to start, because a detector that has not been seen to fire proves nothing by staying silent.
Every run, three independent checks: zero hook events in Claude Code's own stream, no canary file, and zero hooks in its debug log's registry.
Any one failing stops the eval.
A process audit, every 200 ms, of every process descended from each agent, flagging sound players (afplay, say, osascript and the like).

The sandbox held: every package-manager command in the agent's Bash calls must reach the suite's shims (real npm sits in /opt/homebrew/bin on macOS and a login shell can put it first); a run where they did not is not counted and stops the eval.

In the recorded evals: the positive control fired (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SessionEnd canaries, four hook events) before each eval; across the 90 runs there were 0 hook events, 0 canary files and 0 registered hooks; 97 package-manager commands produced 88 shim calls and no run bypassed the shims; and 4,573 process samples saw no sound player.

What an eval cannot tell you.
The suite is what it measures: three synthetic tasks written for these memories, so the results are a demonstration of the method, not of Claude in general.
Five runs per arm per task detect only large effects; narrow the suite with --tasks to put all 30 runs where the memory matters.
Both arms get the memory files appended to the system prompt; Claude Code itself loads the index and reads files on demand, so this is a close stand-in, not the same thing.
The cost is real: $0.72 to $0.82 at API prices and four to seven minutes per 30-run eval with Sonnet 5, on a shared and busy laptop, under your own login.
A new memory can be right and still leave an old one saying the opposite.

When the v2 API goes live, "keep the /v1 compatibility tests green" becomes wrong, and an agent told both things will follow whichever it read last. dreaming check (and every dreaming run, when the model is installed) compares each pending proposal, sentence by sentence, with every other memory and every other pending proposal:

sentences from different files are paired when they share at least two content words, a cheap stand-in for "about the same thing", which contradiction requires (de Marneffe, Rafferty and Manning, 2008);

each pair goes both ways through a natural-language-inference cross-encoder, cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-xsmall (DeBERTa-v3, He, Gao and Chen, 2021, fine-tuned on SNLI and MultiNLI), in its int8 ONNX form, running in WebAssembly in Node on your machine: nothing leaves it;
a pair is a contradiction when either direction puts 0.8 or more of its probability on "contradiction" (chosen before measuring).
The review shows both sentences side by side, marked inferred: the model is small and the decision is yours.

How good it is, on a labelled set of 62 synthetic memory pairs (26 contradictions, 22 compatible, 14 unrelated; test/fixtures/contradictions.json, measured by scripts/contradiction-accuracy.mjs into docs/contradiction-accuracy.json):
As shipped (two shared words, then the threshold) · 0.821 · 0.885 · 0.852
The first version (one shared word) · 0.758 · 0.962 · 0.847
The classifier alone, every pair (AUROC 0.872) · 0.619 · 1.000 · 0.765

The two-word rule was added after the first version called "Staging key for the tidepool smoke test" a contradiction of "the v1 compatibility tests were removed" (0.99), on the word "test" alone; the labelled set was seen while choosing it, so treat its numbers as optimistic.

Its remaining errors are the ones you would expect: the same words about different subjects ("use npm in the legacy billing repo" against "use pnpm in tidepool"), and some entailments read as contradictions.

The model is a download, done properly. dreaming models install states the size and source first (95.9 MB from huggingface.co, pinned to revision 2a4f614), asks, shows progress, checks every file's SHA-256 before it is renamed into place, cancels cleanly with Ctrl-C (nothing partial is left behind), and keeps the files already finished for the next attempt.
Without the model everything works except this check, and the review and the dream say so. dreaming models --verify re-hashes it.
The runtime (onnxruntime-web and @huggingface/tokenizers, about 150 MB) is an optional dependency, loaded only by the check.
The model loads in about a second; a check of the demo's five proposals takes about four seconds on a busy laptop.
dreaming review is laid out like a pull request.

At the top is the list of proposals, one row each, like the changed files of a PR: your decision so far (○ pending, ✓ approved, ✗ rejected), the action, the file, the memory type, the agent's confidence, how many of its evidence quotes verified, the lines it adds and removes, and the checks' marks: ▲ measured to help, ▼ measured to make something worse, ≠ contradicts another memory.
Below it is the selected proposal:
Why: the agent's reason, in one line.
Evidence: each quote with its verdict first (✓ verified, ✗ not found), the session, its working directory and the transcript line, then the transcript's own text for the quoted span.
If the agent elided part of a quote with ..., you see what it left out.
Measured: what dreaming eval found, per task (high-tide 5/5 → 0/5), with the overall change and its interval, the reason a run failed, and the command to replay it; or how to measure it.
Conflicts: what the contradiction check found, both sentences side by side and marked inferred, and whether the memory has changed since the check; or how to run it.
Memory: the one-line description that goes into MEMORY.md.
The diff: every file the approval would touch, line-numbered, with the changed words highlighted, including the pointer line in MEMORY.md.
Each diff accounts for what you have already approved above it.
a / r / s · Approve, reject, skip (leave it in the inbox for later)
u · Undo the decision
e · Edit the memory in $EDITOR; the diff shows your version
→ n / ← p · Next / previous proposal
↓ j / ↑ k, space b · Scroll, page
enter · Submit: the combined diff of everything you approved
? / q · All keys / quit (asks before discarding decisions)
A proposal measured to make a task worse also gets a warning at the top.
Nothing is written until you submit and confirm the combined diff.
Approval is refused, with the reason on screen, when evidence did not verify, when two approvals touch the same memory in conflicting ways, or when the file has changed since the agent read it.
A proposal that would save a redaction marker such as [REDACTED:anthropic-key] into memory is flagged: the agent never saw the secret, so the memory can only hold the placeholder.
dreaming review --plain asks about one proposal at a time, line by line, for pipes, scripts and screen readers; it is used automatically when input or output is not a terminal.
The full-screen review needs at least 50×14 and says so on anything smaller.

A real run costs one headless Claude Code session.
Set agent.model and agent.maxBudgetUsd in the config to control it.
Proposals.
The agent returns JSON: a one-line summary and up to 25 proposals.

Each is an add (new memory), update (replace an existing memory's description, type and body) or delete, with a reason, one to five evidence quotes that each name a session (S1, S2, ...), and a confidence of low, medium or high.
The JSON Schema in the prompt is generated from the same zod schema that validates the reply.
Memory format.

Approved changes are written the way Claude Code reads them: one Markdown file per memory with name, description and metadata.type frontmatter, and one pointer line per memory in MEMORY.md (- [Title](file.md) — description).

An update splices the new description and type into the existing frontmatter text at the positions the YAML parser reports, so every other byte (keys, comments, flow lists, indentation, line endings) is kept; a key the file lacks is added on a new line.
Pointer edits keep each line of MEMORY.md as it was, including its line ending.
Files.
Everything dreaming owns lives under ~/.dreaming (or $DREAMING_HOME), with files readable only by you:
config.json · Validated configuration (see below)
state.json · The watermark: per transcript, the modification time and number of complete lines last read
inbox/<run>.json, inbox/<run>.md · One record per run, plus a Markdown view
runs/<run>/ · Prompt, digests and the agent's output (redacted); removed after a successful run
backups/<apply>/ · Copy of the memory directory's Markdown files, taken before each apply
evals/<eval>.json · Every eval: plan, isolation evidence, and each run with its outcome, turns, tokens and time; statistics are recomputed from it
checks/<run>.json · Contradiction checks for a dream's proposals, with a hash of the memory they were checked against
models/ · The NLI model, if installed here (<id>/<revision>/<file>)
applied.jsonl · Audit log: one line per applied proposal (when, what, before/after hashes, reason, evidence and the sessions it cites); dreaming why reads it
logs/dreaming.log · Output of scheduled runs (launchd and cron)
The agent never writes.

Read-only access is enforced in layers on the claude command line. --restricted confines Claude Code's file tools to the run workspace and the memory directory and ignores user and project settings files, so hooks and plugins configured there do not run. --tools Read,Glob,Grep means no other built-in tool exists in the session; --allowedTools approves only those three; --permission-mode dontAsk denies anything unapproved instead of prompting; --disallowedTools names the built-in tools that write, execute, fetch or delegate, as a backstop; and --strict-mcp-config with no MCP config loads no MCP server.
A test asserts the exact argv, and dreaming run --dry-run prints it.
The only code that writes to the memory directory is the apply step, and it runs only after a person confirms a diff.
Evidence is checked, not trusted.

Each quote must appear in a single message of the session it cites, starting and ending on word and character boundaries ("safe to deploy" does not verify against "unsafe to deploy", and a match never splits a letter from its accents or an emoji sequence).

Matching ignores differences models introduce when copying (whitespace, typographic quotes and dashes, surrounding quotation marks) and accepts ... between fragments that appear in order within 1,000 characters.
Because an elision can drop a word that matters, the reviewer is shown the transcript's own text for the whole matched span, not the agent's rendering of it, together with the transcript line.
A proposal with a quote that cannot be found is blocked and cannot be approved without --allow-unverified.
Verification proves the quote exists; whether the proposal follows from it is still the reviewer's call.
A strict contract, no repair.

The reply must be one JSON object matching the schema, either bare or as the only content of a single json code fence. dreaming does not search prose for JSON or patch near-misses: a reply that broke the contract is a run someone should look at.
The agent's output (redacted) and the prompt are kept in runs/<run>/, the exit code is non-zero, and the watermark does not move, so the next run retries the same sessions.
The output is saved as soon as the agent exits, so a later failure cannot lose a paid reply.
A watermark per session, not per run. state.json records each transcript's modification time and number of complete lines when it was last read.
A single "last run" timestamp silently loses sessions that were still active during a run, and re-reads whole sessions that were resumed.

Per-session marks handle both: active sessions are picked up once they settle, resumed sessions are read from where the last dream stopped, a line still being written is not counted until it is complete, and a run capped by maxSessions leaves the rest for the next one.
Never overwrite a person's edits.
Each update or delete carries the hash of its target as the agent saw it.
If the file has changed since, the proposal is blocked as stale.
The apply step re-reads every file just before writing and refuses if anything differs from the diff that was shown.

Writes are atomic (temp file, fsync, rename), the memory directory is backed up first, and if any write or the audit append fails, every file already written is restored, any partial audit line is removed, and the error says so.
Idempotent by construction.
Applying compares the desired end state with what is on disk, rather than replaying a log.
Re-applying an applied proposal changes nothing and is recorded as already-applied.
That also covers a crash between writing memory and updating the inbox: the next review shows the proposal as already in place and records it.
Redaction in both directions.

Session text is redacted before the agent sees it, and every free-text string the agent returns (summary, reasons, descriptions, bodies, quotes) is redacted again before it is stored; names and file targets are restricted to slug and file-name shapes.

The patterns cover common credential shapes (cloud, model-provider and SaaS API keys, tokens, JWTs, private keys, bearer and basic auth headers, cookies, URL credentials, password=-style assignments) plus long random-looking strings.
They favour over-redaction.

Quoted values are always redacted in full; an unquoted value that is plainly code is left alone (a type name, a $VAR reference, a read from a well-known root such as process.env, or a function call such as z.string()), since coding sessions are full of them.
Every pattern is bounded so a hostile transcript cannot stall a run, and the repository's own files pass the redactor (a test checks).
Extra patterns can be added in the config.
Redactions in the agent's reply are counted apart from those in the transcripts, and the run says so when there are any: a secret-shaped string the agent wrote is worth knowing about.
In review, a proposal that would save a redaction marker into memory is flagged.
Transcripts are untrusted input.
Sessions can contain text from web pages, files and tool output, including text written to manipulate an agent.
The prompt tells the agent that digests are data, not instructions; the agent cannot act on anything it reads; its output is schema-checked; and every change goes past a person.

Agent text containing control characters or invisible Unicode (zero-width, bidirectional-override and tag characters) is rejected outright, so nothing can reach a memory file that the reviewer could not see.
Terminal output is stripped of escape sequences, and the Markdown inbox puts agent text in code fences, so a previewer never renders an agent-supplied link, image or HTML.
dreaming does not dream about itself.
The agent runs with --no-session-persistence, and any session whose working directory is inside the dreaming home is skipped, so tomorrow's run does not read tonight's prompt.
Small surface.
Three runtime dependencies (zod for validation, yaml for frontmatter, diff for unified diffs).

There is no TUI framework: the full-screen review writes to the terminal directly (raw keys, the alternate screen, whole-frame redraws), and one review model drives both it and --plain, so tests drive the same decisions through either front end.
Confidence is a three-level label rather than a number, because a model's stated probability is not calibrated and a decimal would suggest it is.
Any terminal, any width.
Every screen is laid out for the terminal it is in.
On a narrow one, list columns drop, text wraps at word breaks under its label, and the live clock shortens rather than wrapping (a wrapped line cannot be redrawn in place).

Commands and paths are never cut, because a cut command cannot be pasted and run; the dry run prints the agent command one flag per line, and a test feeds it to /bin/sh to prove it reads back as the same arguments.
Colour only repeats what the text already says, so with NO_COLOR every mark and word stays and only the highlighting goes.
The only thing that moves is the elapsed clock while the agent works.

A deterministic grammar extracts assertions.
Literal command patterns choose the newest matching command, by start time with ledger order breaking ties.
Command prefixes, or trusted labels for aggregate verification, select a kind; labels alone do not prove success.

The ledger is .receipts/ledger.jsonl; .receipts/checkpoint.json records its count and terminal hash. check, ls, show and annotate validate integrity before using any evidence. run refuses to execute when existing evidence is corrupt.
VERIFIED · A matching command exited zero against the current fingerprint, without changing it. Numeric claims also agree with a recognized output summary.
STALE · It exited zero, but code changed since or during execution.
FAILED · The latest matching command exited nonzero or was terminated by a signal. An older success does not hide it.
MISMATCH · A claimed number differs from the parsed output.
UNBACKED · No matching command exists, or the numeric summary cannot be established.
VAGUE · Undefined verification scope; always requires human review and fails strict checking.
VAGUE means an assertion such as “Everything is green” or “All green” names no definite checks.
It always requires human review and fails --strict, even if every recorded command succeeded.
It never carries a receipt reference.
Replace it with specific, checkable assertions.
Precedence is FAILED → STALE → numeric evidence → VERIFIED once a command is selected.
A numerical mismatch on stale code is reported as STALE.
Missing numerical evidence is UNBACKED.
The checker does not search backward for a more flattering result.

facts.text: These are exact-span, kind and numeric-value measurements.
A wrong span counts as both a false positive and a false negative.
The broad runs each differed on five messages: two span differences, two unsupported forms, and one non-assertion misclassified as a result.
The focused run differed on one coordinated phrase, “All 28 tests and the build passed”.
The narrower focused score is not directly comparable with the broader scores.
These are curated synthetic examples from a feature brief, not random samples of real agent language or production accuracy.
Exact message overlap with the tuning and previously exposed sets was removed at each first measurement: one, three and zero messages respectively.
The failures were then promoted into tuning and repaired.
All three original files remain byte-for-byte frozen and now serve as regression data.
The current grammar matches all 72, 84 and 48 messages under the explicit current classification policy: five former VAGUE targets are now verification claims.
That versioned projection changes only those kinds, preserving original spans, values and historical gold for the archived measurements.
None remains an untouched accuracy test for the final grammar.
A new blind corpus is needed for another generalization estimate; a later 100% regression score must not replace the first blind score.
The focused score is executable evidence: the frozen extractor exactly matches the pre-inspection source hashes.
The evaluator compiles it, replays its original 28 true positives / 1 false positive / 2 false negatives, and requires that result to match the original report.
The live extractor is tested separately and fixes the exposed case.
Both older broad scores are retained recorded measurements, not replayed against the final grammar.
Inspect the protocols, source hashes and first reports: broad v1, v1 report, v1 sources; broad v2, v2 report, v2 sources; focused, focused report, focused sources.
The user-reported agent-race phrase “Verification passed” is retained separately in the reported regression set, with its supplied ./verify context and provenance.
Its current result is 1 of 1 messages matched (100% precision and recall).
This case was known before the fix: it is neither a blind measurement nor independently observed production evidence.
No transcript or sibling repository was accessed.
npm run eval prints currentRegressions separately from heldOutFirstPass.
The former reruns current code and must have zero false positives and negatives on every corpus for CI to pass.

The latter preserves earlier imperfect measurements and replays the frozen focused extractor. --set tuning checks current tuning only; --set regression checks all former held-out sets with current code; --set held-out validates the archives and replays the first focused score.
Historical failures remain visible; they are not asserted to be current successes.
The v2.1 typography review records the current report styling and monochrome print checks.
The original v2 acceptance report records both visual critique passes, browser results, measured performance and remaining limits.
The report ships zero JavaScript; this is a static evidence document with native controls.

Those are the local checks; CI uses playwright install --with-deps on Ubuntu.
Browser checks are part of npm run gate after browser installation. npm test builds the bin and runs Vitest unit, adversarial, filesystem and executable integration tests.

Tests use synthetic data (plus the explicitly supplied regression phrase) and temporary repositories under ignored .tmp/; no sessions, accounts, remote services or Git commits are needed. npm run eval compiles the archived experiment fixture, checks current regression corpora and reports the recorded blind measurements separately.
It fails on any current regression mismatch, changed frozen bytes or focused replay discrepancy.
See the evaluation section above for provenance and limits.
For contributions, include a minimal synthetic regression for any parser, verdict, fingerprint, redaction or subprocess behavior change.
Add grammar examples and counterexamples to test/fixtures/claims.json; do not edit frozen corpora, snapshots or first reports to improve a metric.
Collect and seal a new unseen set before a future grammar change.
Keep trust boundaries runtime-validated and subprocess arguments out of shell source.
Run the full gate, document changed limits and keep modules small.
Report reproducible defects with synthetic messages and redacted receipts; never attach private transcripts or credentials.
